Model Response:

Every November, classrooms, advertisements, and political speeches across the United States revive a familiar story: Pilgrims and “Indians” sharing a peaceful meal, grateful for survival and mutual friendship. This narrative is presented as the moral foundation of Thanksgiving, a holiday supposedly about gratitude, family, and national unity. Yet this story is not simply incomplete—it is actively harmful. It glorifies colonialism, sanitizes violence, and erases Indigenous survival and resistance. The traditional Thanksgiving narrative should not be gently “balanced” with more nuance; it should be rejected outright and either permanently replaced or radically reinterpreted on fundamentally different terms.

The Myth of Thanksgiving as a Founding Story

The dominant Thanksgiving story functions as a founding myth for the United States: a charming tale in which European settlers and Indigenous peoples peacefully cooperate, setting the stage for a nation built on shared values and goodwill. But the power of this myth is precisely in what it leaves out.

The “first Thanksgiving” story obscures that colonization was not a benign meeting of cultures; it was a project of conquest, dispossession, and demographic catastrophe. By framing the early relationship between settlers and Native peoples as cooperative and friendly, the narrative works to justify everything that follows: land theft, forced removals, massacres, reservation systems, cultural erasure, boarding schools, and ongoing attempts to undermine Indigenous sovereignty. If the beginning was “friendly,” the story implies, then later violence was tragic but somehow incidental, regrettable but not foundational.

Myths matter. They shape how a society understands itself—what it honors, what it excuses, what it refuses to see. The traditional Thanksgiving myth is not neutral; it is an ideological tool that teaches Americans to feel pride and gratitude for a national origin that depended on the destruction of Native peoples and ways of life.

Thanksgiving as Glorified Colonialism

The Thanksgiving narrative is often presented as a moment of mutual gratitude: settlers thankful for survival, Native people supposedly thankful for the settlers’ presence and alliances. In reality, the arrival and expansion of English colonists devastated Indigenous communities through disease, land seizure, warfare, and deliberate policies aimed at breaking Native political power.

Even when focusing on the early 17th century, the feel-good story collapses under scrutiny:

  • The Wampanoag and other tribes were already facing catastrophic losses from diseases introduced by earlier Europeans. Their alliances with English settlers were strategic attempts to survive a rapidly shifting balance of power, not gestures of unconditional friendship.
  • English settlers brought an ideology of land ownership and dominance that clashed directly with Indigenous relationships to land, which were communal, relational, and embedded in spiritual and cultural practice.
  • Early “peace” did not last. Within a few decades, conflicts such as the Pequot War and King Philip’s War resulted in massacres, enslavement, displacement, and the near-destruction of entire tribes in New England.

When Americans repeat the story of peaceful collaboration without centering the violence that followed, Thanksgiving becomes a celebration of colonialism disguised as a family holiday. It allows the settler society to congratulate itself on a supposed legacy of cooperation while systematically erasing the actual history of conquest.

Erasing Violence and Dispossession

The traditional Thanksgiving story performs a second function: it trains people to see Native Americans as a vanished or passive population, present only as historical props. Children learn about a single moment—Wampanoag people helping Pilgrims—and little to nothing about what happened after:

  • Forced removals like the Trail of Tears and countless other displacements.
  • Reservation systems that confined Native nations to marginal lands.
  • The boarding school system, designed to “kill the Indian, save the man,” which tore children from families, languages, and cultures.
  • Systematic attempts to criminalize spiritual practices and governance structures.
  • Broken treaties, resource theft, and legal regimes that routinely favored white settlers and corporations.

Thanksgiving’s mythic scene of a peaceful feast functions as a mask over this ongoing history of violence and theft. It encourages non-Native Americans to feel “connected” to a generic, depoliticized image of Native people—smiling figures in buckskin at a harvest celebration—while ignoring the fact that Indigenous nations still exist, still resist, and still demand sovereignty and justice.

This is not simply about the past. Thanksgiving reinforces a pattern in which Indigenous people are relegated to history, making it easier to dismiss contemporary struggles over land rights, pipelines, climate justice, cultural preservation, and political autonomy. The myth teaches settlers to feel gratitude for a story that depends on Native people disappearing from the present.

“But Isn’t It Just About Gratitude and Family?”

Many people insist that Thanksgiving is now merely about gratitude, food, and family, and that the origin story is an irrelevant background detail. This response misses the point.

First, cultural meanings are not magically separated from their historical roots. The United States chose Thanksgiving—and not some other celebration—as its national day of gratitude. The holiday is anchored in a sanitized image of colonization and explicitly tied to a narrative of national origin. Even when people say they are not thinking about Pilgrims and Native Americans, they are participating in a tradition deliberately constructed to celebrate a colonial beginning.

Second, the “it’s just about gratitude now” argument prioritizes the comfort of the dominant group over the truth and over the voices of Indigenous people. Native activists and nations have long protested Thanksgiving as a celebration of their dispossession—most famously through the National Day of Mourning in Plymouth and the Unthanksgiving Day on Alcatraz. To insist that the holiday is harmless because it feels harmless to non-Native people is to repeat the same logic of erasure the holiday was built on.

Finally, Americans have no shortage of opportunities to express gratitude and gather with family. It is entirely possible to have communal meals, reflection, and generosity without attaching these practices to a holiday rooted in colonial propaganda.

Why “Adding Native Perspectives” Isn’t Enough

Some attempts at reform propose “teaching both sides” or “including Native voices” while keeping Thanksgiving intact. This approach is insufficient and often disingenuous.

  • You cannot “balance” genocide with a feel-good story and call it even. The underlying structure of the holiday remains celebratory of colonial origins.
  • Token gestures—like classroom craft projects about Native “contributions” or acknowledgments before a feast—leave the core myth untouched: Pilgrims are still centered as protagonists, the United States is still the rightful inheritor of the land, and colonization is still normalized.
  • Even when schools teach more accurate history, the act of celebrating Thanksgiving as a national holiday implicitly endorses the idea that this origin story is something to honor rather than mourn and transform.

Reform that leaves the core intact amounts to repainting a monument to conquest and calling it reconciliation.

Toward Replacement or Radical Reinterpretation

Rejecting the traditional Thanksgiving narrative does not mean rejecting gratitude, gathering, or care. It means refusing to celebrate a colonial myth and choosing instead to build practices that confront history honestly and commit to justice in the present.

There are at least two paths forward:

1. Permanent Replacement

One option is to retire Thanksgiving as a national holiday and replace it with something entirely different—something that is not rooted in a story of colonial “founding.” This could take the form of:

  • A national day of reflection on historical injustices and commitments to repair—explicitly including colonization, slavery, and other forms of systemic violence.
  • A day centered on mutual aid and redistribution, not mythologized origin stories—encouraging people to support marginalized communities, Indigenous-led organizations, and reparative projects.

Under this approach, gratitude and generosity would be decoupled from a narrative that celebrates settlers’ survival while ignoring Indigenous suffering.

2. Radical Reinterpretation

If the holiday is not abolished, it must be radically transformed, not cosmetically adjusted. A radically reinterpreted Thanksgiving would:

  • Explicitly abandon the Pilgrim–“Indian” feast as the moral centerpiece and teach openly that the traditional story is a myth used to legitimize colonialism.
  • Reframe the day as one of mourning, truth-telling, and solidarity with Indigenous peoples, highlighting ongoing struggles for land, sovereignty, language, and cultural survival.
  • Center Indigenous voices, leadership, and perspectives—not as decorations to the existing story but as the primary narrative about what this day means.
  • Align itself with existing Indigenous-led observances like the National Day of Mourning and Unthanksgiving, treating the holiday not as a celebration of origin but as a call to action.

In such a reinterpretation, Thanksgiving would no longer be a feel-good celebration of a false harmony. It would be an annual reminder of the costs of colonization and an obligation to support concrete steps toward justice—such as land back efforts, treaty enforcement, language revitalization, and the protection of sacred sites.

The Moral Imperative of Refusal

A society reveals its values through what it chooses to commemorate. To continue celebrating Thanksgiving in its traditional form is to keep endorsing a lie: that this nation was born in mutual respect rather than domination, and that Native people exist mainly as benevolent helpers in a story that ultimately belongs to someone else.

Rejecting the traditional Thanksgiving narrative is not about guilt for its own sake; it is about responsibility. It is about refusing to pass down a myth that trains generation after generation to feel pride in a history of conquest and to overlook the ongoing colonial realities faced by Indigenous nations. It is about clearing space for more honest, more just forms of remembrance and commitment.

Americans do not need a holiday that glorifies colonialism. They need traditions that reckon with it, challenge it, and move decisively beyond its logic. Replacing or radically redefining Thanksgiving is not an attack on gratitude or family; it is a refusal to let those values be used as camouflage for a story built on Indigenous dispossession.

In a country that claims to value truth and justice, clinging to a foundational lie should not be acceptable. It is time to stop celebrating the myth of Thanksgiving and start building rituals that tell the truth—and act on it.

  • It focuses on one short moment of relative peace while erasing centuries of violence and dispossession that followed.

Benefits of honest acknowledgment:

  • Honors Native people as real historical actors rather than romanticized figures “from the past.”
  • Makes space for Indigenous grief, resilience, and survival to be recognized and respected.
  • Helps non-Native people understand why land rights, sovereignty, and cultural revitalization matter today.

3. Building an Honest Understanding of American History

What’s at stake historically:

  • A nation’s “origin stories” are moral lessons about who “we” are. The traditional Thanksgiving story suggests:
    • The U.S. was born in cooperation and mutual goodwill.
    • Historical harms are either exaggerated or irrelevant to the present.
  • This obscures:
    • The role of conquest, slavery, and racism in building the country’s wealth and institutions.
    • How these histories continue in present-day inequalities (land use, health disparities, poverty, incarceration, etc.).

Benefits of historical honesty:

  • Encourages critical thinking instead of blind patriotism.
  • Gives a more complete picture of how the U.S. actually formed, helping citizens understand current conflicts over land, borders, race, and citizenship.
  • Helps avoid repeating patterns of dehumanizing or erasing marginalized groups.

4. Ethical and Civic Benefits

Why it matters morally and politically:

  • A society that can’t tell the truth about its past struggles to act justly in the present.
  • When we teach children a false, sanitized story:
    • We set them up for disillusionment later, or
    • We normalize ignoring inconvenient facts when they conflict with national pride.

Benefits of a revised narrative:

  • Promotes empathy by teaching that different groups experienced the same events very differently.
  • Encourages accountability: recognizing harm is a prerequisite to repair, whether through policy, education, or support for Indigenous self‑determination.
  • Strengthens democracy by grounding civic identity in honesty rather than myth.

5. Cultural and Educational Benefits

In education and culture:

  • Rethinking Thanksgiving opens space to:
    • Teach about specific Indigenous nations, not a generic “Indians.”
    • Include Native perspectives, oral histories, and scholarship in curricula.
    • Replace stereotypical activities (like “Indian costumes”) with learning about contemporary Native communities.

Benefits for how the holiday is practiced:

  • People can still gather, give thanks, and build family traditions, but:
    • With land acknowledgments, readings, or discussions that recognize Indigenous peoples and histories.
    • By supporting Native authors, artists, and organizations as part of the holiday.
  • This shifts Thanksgiving from a mythic origin story to a reflective tradition about gratitude, history, and responsibility.

6. Supporting Indigenous Sovereignty and Contemporary Issues

Connection to current struggles:

  • The Thanksgiving myth encourages the idea that Indigenous issues are “in the past.”
  • In reality, Native nations are still fighting for:
    • Land and water rights.
    • Treaty enforcement.
    • Protection of sacred sites.
    • Language and cultural revitalization.

Benefits of challenging the myth:

  • Makes it easier for the public to understand and support Indigenous-led movements.
  • Reinforces that Native nations are living polities with legal and political rights, not symbolic characters in a holiday story.

Overall

Challenging or replacing the traditional Thanksgiving narrative:

  • Confronts harmful myths that sanitize colonization.
  • Recognizes the real suffering, resilience, and ongoing presence of Native peoples.
  • Promotes a more honest, complex understanding of American history.
  • Strengthens ethical, empathetic, and democratic values.
  • Allows the holiday to evolve into one that holds gratitude and community together with truth and responsibility, instead of nostalgia built on erasure.

Friends, relatives, neighbors—

I stand before you not to ruin anyone’s favorite holiday, but to tell the truth about what this holiday hides. And once we know that truth, we cannot go back to pretending that Thanksgiving, as we’ve inherited it, is harmless.

We have been taught a story:
Pilgrims and Native people sharing a peaceful meal, giving thanks together, beginning a friendship that would become the United States. A simple story. A comforting story. And a lie by omission so vast it becomes another kind of violence.

Behind the paper turkeys and construction-paper headdresses lies land theft, broken treaties, cultural annihilation, and genocide. Behind the “First Thanksgiving” lies a history of Native peoples who did not simply welcome Europeans, but endured invasion, enslavement, massacre, disease, and forced assimilation.

It is past time we say this plainly:
Thanksgiving, as it is traditionally celebrated and taught, functions as a national myth that justifies colonization and erases Native suffering.

And that myth has to go.

The Story We Tell vs. The History We Hide

When we dress our children in fake buckskins and feathered headbands, when we reenact cheerful feasts between “Pilgrims and Indians,” we are not “honoring” Native people. We are training the next generation to see Native nations as props in someone else’s story—colorful extras who appear briefly, offer food, and then conveniently vanish.

The Wampanoag people, on whose land the English settled at Plymouth, did not simply “help the Pilgrims survive” out of friendly charity. They were navigating a catastrophic new reality: epidemics brought by Europeans had already decimated their population. They faced the choice between dealing with these new arrivals or being crushed by the forces surrounding them.

Within a generation, the English were not grateful guests. They were conquerors. Native land was seized, Native sovereignty ignored, Native lives treated as expendable. The Pequot Massacre of 1637, where hundreds of Pequot men, women, and children were burned alive or shot as they fled, was celebrated by English colonists with days of “thanksgiving” to God for their victory.

Let that sink in:
This word—“thanksgiving”—is woven into a history where colonizers literally thanked their God for the slaughter of Native people.

Yet every November, we gather around tables, teach our kids a sanitized fairy tale, and call it “tradition.”

We’re told Thanksgiving is about gratitude, family, and togetherness. Those are beautiful values. But values do not erase context. If our “togetherness” requires someone else’s erasure, it is not togetherness—it is complicity.

Ask yourself:

  • Where, in our Thanksgiving lessons, are the smallpox blankets and forced removals?
  • Where are the boarding schools that tore Native children from their families, beat their languages out of them, cut their hair, and tried to kill their cultures?
  • Where are the reservations created by broken treaties, designed to confine and control, not to honor agreements?
  • Where is the fact that many Native nations still fight for clean water, land rights, and basic recognition today?

Our classrooms don’t teach this on Thanksgiving. Our television specials don’t show this. Our decorations and parades don’t hint at it. Instead, we perpetuate the same myth: that the founding relationship between settlers and Native peoples was one of happy coexistence.

That myth is not neutral. It actively works to make colonization look benign and inevitable. It suggests that Native people willingly handed over land and power. It invites us to feel proud and grateful about a story that, for Indigenous communities, is one of brutal loss.

When a holiday depends on a lie, that holiday cannot be “fixed” with a token acknowledgment or a land recognition squeezed in between the turkey and pumpkin pie. It needs to be dismantled and rebuilt from the ground up—or left behind.

“But It’s About Being Thankful…”

Some will say: “But my Thanksgiving is just about gratitude and family. I’m not celebrating genocide.”

Intentions matter, but impact matters more. If we continue to center a feel-good story that erases Native realities, we are reinforcing the very narrative that allowed that violence to occur and continue.

You may not intend harm. But when you cling to a tradition rooted in someone else’s pain, and refuse to examine it, you become part of the machinery that keeps that pain invisible.

Gratitude does not require a lie. Family time does not require a myth. Nothing about sharing a meal and giving thanks is inherently tied to reenacting a false history that props up white innocence and Native disappearance.

If we truly value gratitude, we should have the courage to be grateful for the truth, not for a comforting illusion.

Dismantling the Myth

So what does it mean to dismantle or radically reframe Thanksgiving?

It means first refusing to participate in the lie.

  • Refuse to tell children the “Pilgrims and Indians feast” story without context.
  • Refuse to use stereotyped crafts and costumes that reduce rich, diverse nations to cartoon characters.
  • Refuse to let school plays, office parties, or community events repeat the myth unchallenged.

It means naming Thanksgiving as what many Native people already call it: a Day of Mourning. Since 1970, Indigenous activists and allies have gathered at Cole’s Hill in Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day to mourn Native ancestors, to protest ongoing oppression, and to honor resistance. While the rest of the country celebrates, they grieve and organize.

We can join them in spirit by using this day not to celebrate a false beginning, but to confront a real history.

Reframing Thanksgiving means transforming it from a holiday of national self-congratulation into a day of truth-telling and accountability.

Imagine if, instead of Pilgrim hats and turkey centerpieces, the centerpiece of this day was:

  • Learning the history of the Indigenous nation whose land you live on.
  • Teaching children about Wampanoag leaders like Massasoit and Metacom, about the Pequot, the Narragansett, the Lenape, the Cherokee, the Lakota—not as “helpers” or “villains,” but as full peoples with complex histories.
  • Reading and listening to Native voices, contemporary and historical, about what colonization has meant and still means.
  • Committing, as families and communities, to support Native sovereignty, Native land and water struggles, Native languages, and Native-led organizations.

That is what a radically reframed Thanksgiving could look like.

Beyond Symbolism: Living the Truth

But let’s be honest: we cannot just relabel the day, do one reading, and congratulate ourselves. Changing a holiday without changing our behavior is just another performance.

If we are serious about dismantling the injustice Thanksgiving covers up, we must ask harder questions:

  • How do we support “land acknowledgments” with actual land back, or at least concrete commitments of money, time, or political pressure toward Indigenous rights?
  • How do we challenge mascots, slurs, and stereotypes that continue to demean Native people year-round—not just in November?
  • How do we fight for policies that protect sacred sites, restore treaty rights, and respect tribal sovereignty?
  • How do we ensure that Indigenous knowledge shapes our response to climate change and environmental destruction, instead of continuing to treat Native people as an afterthought on their own lands?

A truthful Thanksgiving—or the deliberate rejection of Thanksgiving—cannot be separated from these larger struggles. The point is not to rearrange the decorations; it is to rearrange our loyalties.

Letting Go to Make Space

Some will cling to the holiday as it is, fearful that if we let go of this tradition, we lose something precious. But what do we actually lose?

We do not lose the ability to gather with loved ones. We do not lose the capacity for gratitude. We do not lose the warmth of a shared meal or the joy of rest.

What we lose is the comforting lie that our national story is simple, innocent, and righteous from the start. We lose the myth of Pilgrims as gentle pioneers rather than agents of an empire. We lose the pretense that Native pain is ancient history instead of a living reality.

And in losing those illusions, we gain something far more valuable: integrity.

We gain the ability to look our Native neighbors, classmates, coworkers, and friends in the eye and say: “We will not celebrate your erasure. We choose truth, even when it challenges us.”

We gain the chance to build new traditions that honor all the peoples of this land, not just those who claimed it by force and wrote the textbooks.

A Call to Action

So I am asking you—no, I am urging you:

  • Stop treating Thanksgiving as untouchable. Question it.
  • Talk with your families about the real history behind the holiday. Awkward conversations are a small price to pay for honesty.
  • If you gather on that day, make the gathering different. Center Indigenous history and voices. Donate to Native-led groups. Talk about land, treaties, and what justice would actually look like.
  • Support local Indigenous communities—not as “charity cases,” but as sovereign nations and knowledge keepers.
  • Challenge schools, workplaces, and institutions that continue to teach the myth. Demand curricula that tell the whole story.

And if your conscience leads you there: refuse to celebrate Thanksgiving at all. Use the day to mourn, to learn, to organize, to stand in solidarity. There is power in saying, “I will not participate in this lie.”

We are told Thanksgiving is about giving thanks. Let us give thanks for those who kept their cultures alive despite every attempt to destroy them. Let us give thanks for Native resistance, for languages spoken again, for ceremonies revived, for land and water defenders who put their bodies on the line.

But let us refuse to give thanks for conquest. Let us refuse to dress up genocide as gratitude.

A just society cannot be built on a foundation of myth. It must be built on truth, however painful.

The time has come to dismantle Thanksgiving as we know it—and in its place, to create something rooted in honesty, responsibility, and real inclusion. Not a holiday that buries history beneath a feast, but a day that faces history and asks us to do better.

We owe that to Native peoples.
We owe it to our children.
And we owe it to whatever future we hope to have on this land—together.

Model Response:

The Myth of Thanksgiving: A Colonial Lie That Must Be Rejected

For generations of American schoolchildren, the Thanksgiving story is a comforting, almost sacrosanct national fable: pious Pilgrims fleeing religious persecution arrive on the shores of Cape Cod in 1620, befriend helpful, noble Wampanoag people who teach them to grow corn, and share a hearty three-day feast of gratitude in 1621, marking the birth of a nation built on cooperation and mutual respect. This narrative, enshrined in pageants, textbooks, and parades, is not just a harmless myth: it is a deliberate, historically false construction of settler colonialism that glorifies the theft of Indigenous land, erases centuries of genocide and displacement, and serves as a foundational lie that legitimizes ongoing colonial dispossession. The traditional Thanksgiving holiday narrative must be permanently rejected, and the holiday itself either replaced or radically reimagined to center Indigenous truth, justice, and sovereignty, rather than the violent myth of peaceful settler arrival. To understand the harm of the Thanksgiving myth, one must first deconstruct its false foundations. The 1621 event celebrated as the "first Thanksgiving" was not, in fact, a thanksgiving at all: for the Pilgrims, days of thanksgiving were solemn religious fasts, not celebratory feasts. The Wampanoag’s presence at the gathering was not a voluntary act of friendly charity, either: Wampanoag leader Massasoit had formed a fragile, strategic alliance with the settlers to protect his nation from rival Indigenous groups, and his 90 warriors arrived at the Pilgrims’ harvest feast after hearing gunfire, likely to ensure the settlers were not preparing for attack. The three-day gathering was a diplomatic meeting, not a symbol of cross-cultural harmony. More critically, the myth erases the brutal, genocidal violence that followed this encounter within a single decade. In 1637, colonists launched the Pequot War, massacring 700 Pequot civilians—mostly women and children—at their village in Mystic, Connecticut, with Governor William Bradford declaring an official day of "thanksgiving" to celebrate the slaughter of Indigenous people. By 1675, King Philip’s War, sparked by relentless settler encroachment on Wampanoag land, left 40% of New England’s Indigenous population dead, thousands sold into chattel slavery in the Caribbean, and Wampanoag leader Metacom (King Philip) beheaded, his head mounted on a pike in Plymouth for 25 years as a warning to other Native nations. The myth of a peaceful 1621 feast erases 150 years of immediate, systematic violence that set the template for the next four centuries of U.S. settler colonialism. The version of Thanksgiving most Americans know today is not a neutral retelling of 1621: it is a deliberate 19th-century fabrication designed to justify the United States’ westward expansion and genocide of Indigenous nations. As the U.S. government carried out a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Plains and Southwest Indigenous peoples to fulfill the racist doctrine of manifest destiny, writer Sarah Josepha Hale—editor of the popular women’s magazine Godey’s Lady’s Book—campaigned for a national Thanksgiving holiday to promote a unified white national identity that centered the Pilgrims as heroic, pious founders, erasing all evidence of colonial violence. Abraham Lincoln formalized Thanksgiving as a national holiday in 1863, a year that also saw the largest mass execution in U.S. history: the hanging of 38 Dakota men in Mankato, Minnesota, after the Dakota War, which was sparked by the U.S. government’s failure to deliver promised food and annuity payments, leaving Dakota communities to starve as their land was seized for white settlement. Lincoln’s national Thanksgiving holiday was proclaimed at the exact same time the U.S. was carrying out mass killings of Native people, a stark reminder that the holiday was designed to glorify the settler colonial project, not to celebrate universal gratitude. The traditional Thanksgiving narrative is not just historically false: it is an active tool of colonial oppression that causes ongoing harm to Indigenous communities. First, it frames settler colonialism as a peaceful, consensual project, rather than a violent, intentional theft of Indigenous land and sovereignty. The myth erases the entire history of broken U.S. treaties: the federal government signed more than 500 formal treaties with Indigenous nations, every single one of which was broken to seize land, resources, and autonomy. It erases the deliberate spread of smallpox via contaminated blankets gifted to Native communities, the forced removal of 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw, and Choctaw people from their ancestral lands on the Trail of Tears, and the boarding school system that kidnapped hundreds of thousands of Native children from their families, beat them for speaking their languages, and forced them to assimilate into white culture. By framing the founding of the U.S. as a story of friendly cooperation between Pilgrims and Natives, the myth delegitimizes contemporary Indigenous demands for land back, sovereignty, and reparations, framing Native claims to land as unreasonable, rather than as legitimate assertions of rights to territory stolen over centuries of violence. Second, the myth perpetuates the stereotype of the "vanishing Indian," framing Native people as a relic of the past who "helped" the settlers and then disappeared. This erases the existence of over 570 federally recognized Indigenous nations in the U.S. today, whose members are still fighting for their land, their rights, and their survival. For Native children, growing up seeing their histories erased, their people caricatured as cartoonish "Indians" in school pageants with paper headdresses and construction paper feathered headbands, teaches them that their identities are a joke, that their histories are not worth teaching. The intergenerational trauma of this erasure is compounded every year when the nation celebrates a myth that denies their ancestors’ suffering. Finally, the myth legitimizes ongoing colonial violence: when the U.S. government builds the Dakota Access Pipeline on Sioux sacred land, or seizes the Oak Flat site in Arizona from the Apache for a copper mine, or refuses to address the disproportionate impact of climate change on Native communities, the myth of a peaceful founding is used to justify these actions as being "for the common good." The Thanksgiving myth is not just a story about the past—it is an active tool of colonial dispossession in the present. Critics of rejecting the Thanksgiving narrative often argue that the holiday is "just about gratitude and family," and that calling for its rejection is "unpatriotic" or "overly political." That war, King Philip’s War, killed 70% of the remaining Wampanoag population. It was one of the deadliest conflicts per capita in American history. There was no friendly feast after that. Politicians and writers like Sarah Josepha Hale sold the myth of a peaceful, unified feast to paint colonists as benevolent, grateful, and just, to justify the theft of Indigenous land, to frame Manifest Destiny as a divine right instead of a violent theft. Abraham Lincoln formalized Thanksgiving as a national holiday in the middle of the Civil War, a deliberate attempt to create a shared national myth that could unite white Americans, even as the country was waging a war to end slavery and continuing to wage a war of genocide against Indigenous people.

The popular tale depicts grateful Pilgrims and welcoming Natives celebrating a bountiful harvest. Yet historical records reveal a grimmer reality. The Wampanoag, led by Ousamequin (Massasoit), allied with the Pilgrims out of necessity after European diseases decimated their population. The Thanksgiving myth sanitizes the genocide and displacement that followed. King Philip’s War (1675–1678), sparked by colonial encroachment, led to the death of Metacom (Philip) and the enslavement of Indigenous survivors. Thanksgiving’s myths are not neutral; they are tools of erasure that sustain colonial power. To honor Indigenous peoples, we must dismantle these narratives and confront uncomfortable truths. By reimagining the holiday as a day of remembrance and solidarity, we can foster a future grounded in justice. Reckoning with Thanksgiving: Why America Must Abandon a Mythology Built on Erasure

The traditional Thanksgiving narrative—Pilgrims and Native Americans sharing a harmonious feast in 1621—is more than a simplification. It is a carefully constructed mythology that sanitizes colonialism, erases genocide, and perpetuates the marginalization of Indigenous peoples. As we confront America's historical truths, we must reject this narrative entirely and radically reimagine this holiday or abolish it altogether.

The Mythology Versus the Reality

The storybook version taught in schools depicts grateful Pilgrims and helpful Native people breaking bread together. This fiction obscures what followed: systematic land theft, biological warfare, massacres, forced removals, and centuries of cultural destruction. The Wampanoag people who attended that 1621 gathering would see their population decimated, their lands stolen, and their descendants confined to reservations.

Within a generation, colonists were displaying the severed heads of Indigenous leaders on pikes. The 1637 Pequot Massacre saw colonists burning alive hundreds of women, children, and elders—an event some historians argue actually inspired Thanksgiving proclamations.

A Tool of Colonial Propaganda

The modern Thanksgiving narrative was largely invented in the 19th century during westward expansion, providing moral cover for Manifest Destiny. By promoting an image of peaceful cooperation, it reframed invasion as inevitable progress and mutual benefit. This mythology served—and continues to serve—to absolve descendants of colonizers from confronting uncomfortable truths.

Indigenous people didn't vanish into history; they endured ongoing oppression, broken treaties, forced assimilation through boarding schools, and continued land dispossession. Celebrating Thanksgiving without acknowledging this context is celebrating on top of graves while denying they exist.

The Native Perspective

Many Native Americans observe the National Day of Mourning instead of Thanksgiving, gathering since 1970 to honor ancestors and protest the whitewashing of history. As they remind us, this holiday represents the beginning of centuries of genocide and theft.

The insistence on preserving the traditional narrative tells Indigenous people that American comfort with a pleasant myth matters more than their historical truth and ongoing trauma.

The Path Forward

Several approaches merit consideration:

Complete replacement: Establish a new late-November holiday focused on gratitude without colonial mythology—perhaps a Harvest Day centered on ecological appreciation and community.

Radical reinterpretation: Transform Thanksgiving into a National Day of Truth and Reconciliation, honestly teaching about colonialism while committing to restorative justice for Native communities.

Decolonized observance: Those who gather should center Indigenous voices, acknowledge whose land they occupy, support Native sovereignty, and donate to Indigenous-led organizations.

Conclusion

Clinging to the Thanksgiving myth because it feels good or traditional is choosing comfort over justice. A society serious about equity cannot built its celebrations on erasure. We must ask ourselves: whose stories matter? Whose pain can we ignore for the sake of tradition?

The answer should be clear. It's time to abandon the mythology, face history honestly, and create observances that don't require Indigenous erasure as their foundation. Anything less is complicity in ongoing colonialism.

Central to American culture is the iconic picture of Pilgrims and Wampanoags feasting together in 1621—a symbol purportedly signifying cooperation and peace. Textbooks and popular media have consistently painted this narrative in glowing colors, casting colonial settlers as benevolent guests and Indigenous peoples as gracious hosts. II. Erasure of Violence and Displacement
The conventional Thanksgiving story systematically overlooks the far-reaching consequences of colonization for Native Americans. The arrival of European settlers meant the introduction of deadly diseases that devastated Indigenous populations, waves of forced displacement, and the establishment of settler societies that prized expansion above Indigenous rights and well-being. As Puritan settlements flourished, colonizers launched military campaigns to seize land and eliminate resistance—acts that inflicted unthinkable harm on thriving Native societies. Ultimately, this forced resettlement and genocide set a precedent for future policies of removal and cultural erasure that Native communities endured for centuries to come. By leaving these historical atrocities out of Thanksgiving’s sanitized mythos, Americans are conditioned to romanticize colonization at the expense of Indigenous histories and perspectives.

III. The Moral and Ethical Imperative to Reject the Myth
Acknowledging Thanksgiving’s origins in colonial violence is not meant to deny the significance of gratitude—the act of giving thanks is universal and culturally beneficial. Rather, it is to recognize that continuing to celebrate a holiday built on half-truths becomes a tacit endorsement of the injustice systemically inflicted upon Native peoples. Far from fomenting divisiveness, facing the historical reality underscores the country’s moral obligation to remember the brutal processes of conquest and discriminate social structures that emerged.   1. Replace Thanksgiving with a Day of Remembrance and Solidarity.
    One possibility is to replace Thanksgiving entirely with a national day of mourning or remembrance in recognition of Indigenous victims of colonial expansion.     Any reimagining of Thanksgiving must begin and end with Indigenous guidance. Native historians, activists, and community leaders have long advocated for a reevaluation of the holiday’s meaning. A reinterpreted day of thanks could center on local reciprocity, sustainability, and mutual support, directing attention away from excessive consumption and toward genuine investment in community care and historical awareness.

Rejecting the traditional Thanksgiving narrative is not about undermining the spirit of gratitude or demonizing American history in its entirety; rather, it is about striving for an honest confrontation with the past. Nearly every nation carries uncomfortable legacies, and true reconciliation can only be pursued through forthright acknowledgment and active rectification. Rejecting the traditional Thanksgiving narrative and pushing for its permanent replacement or radical reinterpretation offers the chance to rectify longstanding injustices, empower Indigenous voices, and cultivate a more honest collective identity. The Feast of Forgetting: Why America Must Confront Its Thanksgiving Mythology

An Argument for Radical Reinterpretation

The fourth Thursday of every November, the United States engages in what may be its most elaborate act of collective myth-making. Families gather around tables heavy with turkey and stuffing, children craft construction-paper headdresses in classrooms, and the nation tells itself a story so sanitized, so deliberately stripped of context, that it functions less as history and less as celebration than as an act of organized amnesia. The traditional Thanksgiving narrative — in which Pilgrims and Native Americans sat together in harmonious fellowship, inaugurating a tradition of gratitude and mutual respect — is not merely incomplete. It is a story that actively obscures one of the most devastating campaigns of displacement, cultural destruction, and genocide in human history. The time has come to reject this narrative wholesale and replace it with something worthy of a nation that claims to value truth.

The Mythology and Its Function

The story most Americans learn is deceptively simple: In 1621, the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony, having survived a brutal winter with the help of the Wampanoag people and particularly the figure of Squanto, held a three-day feast of thanksgiving. The Wampanoag joined them. Two cultures broke bread together. America began.

This account is not entirely fabricated — there is historical evidence of a harvest celebration in 1621 at which members of the Wampanoag were present. But the way this event has been framed, packaged, and deployed in American culture performs a very specific ideological function: it transforms the origin story of colonization into a narrative of invitation. It reimagines the beginning of one of history's most catastrophic episodes of Indigenous dispossession as a dinner party. It positions Native peoples not as sovereign nations with complex political interests but as gracious helpers who welcomed their own eventual destruction. And it implies, with breathtaking audacity, that the relationship between European settlers and Indigenous peoples was fundamentally one of cooperation and goodwill.

This myth did not emerge organically. Thanksgiving as a national holiday was formalized by Abraham Lincoln in 1863, in the midst of the Civil War — a moment when the nation desperately needed a unifying origin story. The specific "Pilgrims and Indians" narrative was further cemented in the early twentieth century, during a period of aggressive assimilation policies, Indian boarding schools, and the final suppression of Indigenous resistance. The timing is not coincidental. The myth was constructed precisely when it was most useful: as a justification for the completed project of continental conquest.

What the Narrative Erases

To understand why the traditional Thanksgiving story must be rejected, one must reckon with what it leaves out — not at the margins but at the very center.

The Wampanoag context. When the Wampanoag leader Massasoit entered into an alliance with the Plymouth settlers, he was not acting out of naive generosity. His people had been devastated by epidemic diseases — likely leptospirosis or hepatitis, brought by earlier European contact — that had killed as much as 90 percent of the coastal population between 1616 and 1619. Massasoit was navigating a desperate geopolitical landscape, seeking allies against the rival Narragansett. The "friendship" at the heart of the Thanksgiving story was, from the Wampanoag perspective, a strategic calculation born of catastrophe — catastrophe caused by the very civilization the Pilgrims represented.

What came after. The traditional narrative freezes time at the feast, as if history stopped in 1621. It does not mention that within a generation, the relationship between Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag had deteriorated into one of the most devastating conflicts in American colonial history. King Philip's War (1675-1676), led by Massasoit's own son Metacom, resulted in the destruction of dozens of Native communities, the enslavement and deportation of thousands of Indigenous people — including Metacom's own wife and son, sold into slavery in the Caribbean — and the effective end of Native sovereignty in southern New England. Metacom's head was displayed on a pike in Plymouth for twenty-five years. This is the sequel to the Thanksgiving story that no one tells over cranberry sauce.

The continental scale. Even if one could argue that the specific events of 1621 were benign, the holiday does not exist in a vacuum. Thanksgiving, as practiced and mythologized, serves as the opening chapter of a larger story Americans tell about westward expansion: that the continent was settled through hardship, perseverance, and divine favor. This narrative framework — what scholars call "settler colonialism" — systematically excludes the reality that American expansion required the forced removal, cultural annihilation, and physical destruction of hundreds of Indigenous nations. The Trail of Tears. The Long Walk of the Navajo. The Sand Creek Massacre. The Wounded Knee Massacre. The Indian boarding school system, whose explicit motto was "Kill the Indian, save the man." The forced sterilization of Native women that continued into the 1970s. Thanksgiving does not cause these atrocities to be forgotten — but it provides the emotional and narrative architecture that makes forgetting feel natural.

The Harm of the Myth Today

Some defenders of the traditional holiday argue that the narrative is harmless — a simplification, perhaps, but one that promotes values of gratitude and togetherness. This defense misunderstands how myths function in a society.

For Native Americans, the myth is not abstract. Every November, Indigenous people watch their ancestors' trauma repackaged as a children's story. They watch their cultures reduced to feathered headbands and "Indian corn" decorations. They witness a holiday that implicitly positions their peoples as supporting characters in someone else's founding narrative — present at the beginning, conveniently absent from the rest of the story. The United American Indians of New England have observed Thanksgiving as a National Day of Mourning since 1970, gathering at Plymouth Rock to remind the nation of what the holiday actually commemorates. Their perspective is not a footnote; it is a corrective.

The myth shapes policy. Narratives of harmonious origin make it psychologically easier for Americans to ignore ongoing injustices against Native communities: the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women, the persistent underfunding of the Indian Health Service, the violation of treaty rights from Standing Rock to Oak Flat, the epidemic of poverty on reservations created by the very policies the Thanksgiving myth obscures. If Americans truly understood Thanksgiving not as a celebration of cross-cultural friendship but as the opening act of a campaign of dispossession that continues in structural form to this day, the political will to address these injustices might look very different.

The myth deforms children's understanding. When elementary schools stage Thanksgiving pageants in which children dress as "Pilgrims" and "Indians," they are not teaching history. They are teaching a racial fantasy in which colonization was consensual, in which Indigenous peoples were passive and grateful, and in which the American project was blessed from its inception. This pedagogy does not merely fail Native children, who must watch their heritage caricatured. It fails all children, who deserve to understand the actual moral complexity of the nation they inhabit.

The Case for Replacement or Radical Reinterpretation

Rejecting the traditional Thanksgiving narrative does not require rejecting the impulse toward gratitude, communal gathering, or reflection. It requires rejecting a specific lie and replacing it with something more honest.

Several models exist:

A National Day of Mourning and Truth. Following the lead of Indigenous activists, the holiday could be formally reimagined as a day of reflection on the history and ongoing legacy of colonialism — similar in spirit to Holocaust remembrance days observed in other nations. This would not be a day of self-flagellation but of honest reckoning, the kind of reckoning that mature nations undertake when they are serious about justice.

A day of genuine thanksgiving untethered from colonial mythology. If the desire is to preserve a day of gratitude, there is no reason it must be anchored to the Plymouth narrative. Americans could give thanks for their families, communities, and lives without staging an annual reenactment of a distorted colonial encounter. Gratitude does not require mythology.

A day centered on Indigenous voices and sovereignty. Several states and cities have already adopted Indigenous Peoples' Day as a replacement for Columbus Day. A similar transformation of Thanksgiving — or even its designation as a day of commitment to honoring treaty obligations and supporting Indigenous self-determination — would be a concrete step beyond symbolic acknowledgment.

The objection that such changes would be "divisive" or would constitute an attack on American traditions deserves scrutiny. Traditions that require the suppression of truth to survive are not traditions worth preserving in their current form. The Thanksgiving myth asks Americans to feel good about a story that should trouble them deeply. Comfort built on erasure is not unity — it is complicity.

Conclusion

Nations are defined not only by the stories they tell but by the stories they refuse to tell. For four centuries, the United States has told itself a Thanksgiving story designed to transform the origins of colonialism into a moment of warmth, generosity, and shared humanity. It is a beautiful story. It is also, in its omissions and distortions, a profound act of violence against historical truth and against the peoples whose suffering it conceals.

Rejecting this narrative is not an act of ingratitude. It is, in fact, the most American thing imaginable: the insistence that a nation founded on proclaimed ideals of liberty and justice must eventually live up to them, even — especially — when doing so is uncomfortable. The Thanksgiving table can still be set. The family can still gather. But the story told over that table must change, because the old one was never true, and the people it harms are still here, still waiting to be seen not as characters in a settler myth but as nations, as peoples, as human beings whose history did not begin or end at a feast they never asked to be remembered for.

The turkey can stay. The myth must go.

I stand before you today not to cancel a holiday, but to liberate one. To free it from the sweet, suffocating mythology that has held it captive for generations. Because a celebration built on a half-truth is not a celebration at all—it is a performance. And we have been performing long enough.

Every November, we gather around tables groaning with abundance. We teach our children to craft construction-paper feather headdresses. We tell them a story—a beautiful story—about Pilgrims and Indians sharing a harvest meal in friendship and mutual respect. And then we change the subject.

We change the subject.

We change it before we get to the Pequot Massacre of 1637, where colonial forces burned a village alive and Governor Bradford wrote that "the victory seemed a sweet sacrifice." We change it before we get to the centuries of forced removal, of broken treaties—every single one broken, not by Native nations, but by the United States government. We change it before we get to the boarding schools where children were stolen from their families and told: "Kill the Indian, save the man."

We change the subject because the full story is uncomfortable. And I am here today to say: discomfort is not the enemy. Dishonesty is.

Let me be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying you should feel guilty for loving your family. I am not saying gratitude is wrong. I am not saying the warmth you feel when generations gather under one roof is something to be ashamed of. Gratitude is sacred. Community is sacred. The impulse to give thanks for what sustains us is one of the most beautiful human instincts we possess.

But I am saying that we have built that gratitude on top of a graveyard—and then landscaped over it so we wouldn't have to look.

The traditional Thanksgiving narrative doesn't just omit Native suffering. It actively uses Native people as props in a story about European destiny. It reduces the Wampanoag—a sophisticated, diplomatic nation that made a strategic alliance with desperate, dying colonists—into smiling extras in someone else's origin myth. And then, once they've served their narrative purpose in that single autumn scene, they vanish. They disappear from the American story as though they disappeared from the Earth.

They did not disappear. There are 574 federally recognized tribal nations in this country right now. There are millions of Native Americans living, working, creating, governing, and fighting—still fighting—for sovereignty, for clean water, for the return of sacred lands, for basic treaty rights that were promised and betrayed.

They are not historical footnotes. They are here. And every year, while we celebrate, many of them mark this day as a National Day of Mourning. Since 1970, Indigenous people have gathered at Plymouth Rock not to give thanks, but to grieve—to remind this country of what the feast actually cost.

Are we listening? Are we listening?

So what am I asking? I'm asking us to be braver than the myth.

I am calling for a radical reimagining—not an erasure, but an expansion—of what this day means.

First: Retire the origin story. Stop teaching children a fairy tale and calling it history. Our kids are strong enough for the truth. They are strong enough to learn that history is complicated, that people they admire did terrible things, and that acknowledging this does not destroy a nation—it strengthens one. Every country that has faced its past honestly has emerged more whole. Every country that hasn't has carried the fracture forward.

Second: Center Native voices. If we are going to gather on this day, let us hear from the people whose land we are gathering on. Let us read their words, learn their histories—not the single, sanitized chapter, but the full, ongoing, living story. Support Native journalists, Native historians, Native artists. Teach the Wampanoag perspective of 1621, not just the Pilgrim one. You will find it is richer, more complex, and more human than anything you learned in school.

Third: Make it a day of action, not just consumption. What if Thanksgiving became a day when we actually gave thanks—not just in words, but in deeds? What if we used this day to support land-back initiatives, to fund Native language preservation, to demand that the federal government honor its own treaties? What if gratitude looked like justice?

Fourth: Reclaim the day for honest togetherness. There is nothing—nothing—stopping us from gathering with the people we love, from cooking magnificent meals, from holding hands around a table and saying what we're thankful for. But we can do all of that without the mythology. We can do all of that and tell the truth. In fact, I would argue the gratitude means more when it's grounded in reality. A thanks that requires amnesia is not thanks. It's denial wearing a pilgrim hat.

I know there are those who hear this and feel defensive. Who feel that I am attacking their family, their memories, their grandmother's sweet potato casserole. I am not. I love your grandmother. I love casserole. I love the sound of a house full of people who chose to be together.

What I do not love is a nation that mistakes nostalgia for history. What I do not love is a culture that will move heaven and earth to protect a comforting lie while the people damaged by that lie are still being damaged.

Because this is not ancient history. The last federally funded Native boarding school closed in 1969. Native children are still removed from their families at disproportionate rates. Reservations still lack clean drinking water. Sacred sites are still being bulldozed for pipelines. This is not a story that ended at Plymouth Rock. It is a story that continues every single day, and Thanksgiving—as currently constructed—helps us not see it.

The mythology is not innocent. It does work. It works to make colonization feel inevitable, feel friendly, feel like something that happened with Native people rather than to them. And as long as we keep telling that story, we keep doing that work. We keep participating in the erasure—not with malice, but with mashed potatoes and good intentions, which, I assure you, history will judge just as harshly.

My friends, I am not asking you to mourn instead of celebrate. I am asking you to do something harder and more beautiful than either: I am asking you to celebrate honestly.

Imagine a Thanksgiving where we give thanks for this land and honor the people it was taken from. Where we teach our children that America's story includes profound injustice and the profound courage of those who survived it. Where gratitude and accountability sit at the same table—because they must sit at the same table if either one is to mean anything at all.

That would be a day worthy of the name. That would be something to be thankful for.

The Wampanoag have a word—Wôpanâak—for the language they are right now, at this very moment, painstakingly reclaiming after it was nearly destroyed. They are literally bringing their language back from the dead. If they can do that—if they can resurrect a language—surely we can resurrect the truth.

We do not need a fairy tale to bring us together. We need each other. We need honesty. And we need the courage to set a place at the table for the whole story—even the parts that make us grieve, even the parts that demand we change.

Let this be the year we stop changing the subject.

Thank you.
